name: Double Kerr Solution
description: Two Kerr black holes on one axis of symmetry, the stationary vacuum solution Dietrich Kramer and Gernot Neugebauer built in 1980 by two Bäcklund transformations of flat space. The repulsion between the spins does not balance the attraction of the masses, so a strut on the axis between the horizons holds the holes apart.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Set two black holes side by side at rest. What keeps them from falling together? Two Schwarzschild bodies on one axis were the first attempt, by Rudolf Bach and Hermann Weyl in 1922, and Bach found the stretch of axis between the bodies singular [bach1922, neugebauer2012]. Weyl read the singularity as a stress along the axis, a push from outside gravity that makes up for the attraction of the two bodies [bach1922, neugebauer2012]. By Robert Wald's calculation of 1972, two spinning bodies also act on each other through their spins, with a force of the same form as the one between two magnets and the opposite sign, so that "north pole" attracts "north pole" [wald1972]. Two bodies spinning the same way about the line that joins them therefore repel, and the spins might do the work of the strut [herdeiro2008, neugebauer2012].¶For a stationary field with an axis of symmetry the vacuum equations come down to one equation for one complex potential, which Frederick Ernst wrote in 1968 [ernst1968, neugebauer2012]. A Bäcklund transformation for it, a rule that makes a new solution out of an old one, came from Gernot Neugebauer in 1979 [neugebauer1979, neugebauer2012]. One use of the rule on flat space returns the Kerr-NUT solution, which contains Kerr's black hole, and two uses return a solution with seven parameters [neugebauer2012]. Dietrich Kramer and Neugebauer published it in 1980 under the title "The superposition of two Kerr solutions" [kramer1980]. Its parameters can be taken as two masses, two angular momenta, the distance between the holes, a NUT charge, and a mass for the stretch of axis between them [herdeiro2008]. In Weyl's coordinates each horizon is a rod lying on the axis [neugebauer2012].¶Do the spins hold the holes apart? The answer sits on the stretch of axis between the two rods, which has to be an ordinary axis, with no closed timelike curves round it and no strut along it [herdeiro2008]. By 1982 Masahiro Kihara and Akira Tomimatsu had proved that in the superposition of two Kerr solutions the stretch between the horizons is a surface with closed timelike curves on it [kihara1982]. Later that year the two wrote down the conditions on the parameters that make the axis regular [tomimatsu1982, neugebauer2012]. Working through those conditions, Cornelius Hoenselaers argued in 1984 that "two non-extreme black holes with positive Komar masses cannot be in stationary equilibrium" [hoenselaers1984]. The proof came in 2001 from Vladimir Manko and Eduardo Ruiz, who had solved the conditions in closed form [manko2001, neugebauer2012].¶Manko and Ruiz had tested one family, and a balanced pair of black holes might still exist outside it [neugebauer2012]. So Neugebauer and Jörg Hennig posed the boundary value problem itself, with two separate horizons, a regular axis, and flat space far away, and found in 2009 that every solution of it belongs to the family [neugebauer2009]. Their test for a black hole was an inequality that Hennig, Marcus Ansorg, and Carla Cederbaum had proved the year before: a horizon with trapped surfaces just inside it has $8\pi|J| < A$, with $J$ its angular momentum, $A$ its area, and $G = c = 1$ [hennig2008, neugebauer2009]. With the axis regular, one of the two horizons breaks the inequality [neugebauer2009]. The case of horizons with zero surface gravity followed in 2011 [hennig2011]. Piotr Chruściel, Michał Eckstein, Luc Nguyen, and Sebastian Szybka then derived the inequality from the regularity of the spacetime out to future null infinity, and stated the outcome as a theorem: "$\mathscr{I}^+$-regular two-Kerr solutions do not exist" [chrusciel2011].¶With the strut kept, the solution holds two black holes still at a separation of one's choosing, and the strut measures the force between them [herdeiro2008]. The simplest pair has equal masses $M$ and opposite angular momenta $J$ and $-J$, with the centres of the two rods a coordinate distance $\zeta$ apart, and Carlos Herdeiro and Carmen Rebelo worked it out in 2008 [herdeiro2008]. There the force is $F = M^2/(\zeta^2 - 4M^2)$ in units with $G = c = 1$, the same as between two Schwarzschild holes, and $J$ does not appear in it [herdeiro2008]. Each hole drags the other's frame, so the horizons turn more slowly the closer the holes stand and stop turning where they touch [herdeiro2008]. A hole in the pair can carry more spin than Kerr's limit of $M^2$, up to $|J| = M^2\sqrt{(\zeta + 2M)/(\zeta - 2M)}$ [herdeiro2008]. Miguel Costa joined Herdeiro and Rebelo in 2009 to follow the ergoregions: those of two holes spinning the same way merge as the holes approach, and those of two holes spinning opposite ways stay apart [costa2009].

related.text: One of the two holes on its own. A single Bäcklund transformation of flat space returns the Kerr-NUT solution, which holds Kerr's black hole, and two return the pair [neugebauer2012].

One hole on its own with the spin switched off. With both spins switched off the pair is Rudolf Bach and Hermann Weyl's two Schwarzschild bodies of 1922, with a singular stretch of axis between them [bach1922, neugebauer2012].

Black holes that do stand still side by side. Each carries a charge equal to its mass, and the electric repulsion balances the attraction, which the repulsion between two spins does not [hartle1972, neugebauer2009].
Spinning sources that do stay in balance. Each carries a charge equal to its mass, and the electric repulsion holds the spinning sources in a stationary configuration [perjes1971, israel1972].

Jean Chazy and H. E. J. Curzon each presented two point particles at rest on one axis, and the line joining the particles is singular as the axis between the two holes is [chazy1924, curzon1925, einstein1936twobody].

Two black holes at rest with no strut between them, for one moment only: the slice of space from which Susan Hahn and Richard Lindquist first computed two holes colliding head on [brill1963, hahn1964, holst2016].

Another solution from Gernot Neugebauer's inverse methods in Jena: a rigidly rotating disc of dust, solved with Reinhard Meinel as a boundary value problem for Ernst's equation fifteen years after the two holes [neugebauer1995, neugebauer2003].
The Bäcklund transformations behind the double Kerr solution coincide with the soliton transformations of Belinski and Zakharov [alekseev2010].

coordinates.name: Weyl-Lewis-Papapetrou
domains: \rho = 0,\; a_1 \le z \le a_2 \;\text{and}\; a_3 \le z \le a_4 \;\text{(the two horizons)}

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, with $-f$ the norm of the Killing vector $\partial_t$ in the chart $x^0 = ct$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $f\left(\partial_\rho^2f + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho f + \partial_z^2f\right) = \left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_zf\right)^2 - \dfrac{f^4}{\rho^2}\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right)$ together with the equations for $\omega$ and $\gamma$; for two Kerr black holes $f$ is the real part of the Ernst potential $\mathcal{E} = D_-/D_+$, with $D_\pm = X^\pm_{12}X^\pm_{34} - X^\pm_{14}X^\pm_{32}$, $X^\pm_{ik} = \dfrac{\alpha_ir_i + \alpha_kr_k}{a_i - a_k} \pm 1$, and $r_j = \sqrt{\rho^2 + (z - a_j)^2}$, where $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, and $a_4$ are the ends of the two horizons on the axis, lengths in increasing order, and each $\alpha_j$ is a complex number of modulus one

Function of $\rho$ and $z$, a length, with $f\omega$ the product of the Killing vectors $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\phi$; in a vacuum $\partial_\rho\left(\dfrac{f^2}{\rho}\partial_\rho\omega\right) + \partial_z\left(\dfrac{f^2}{\rho}\partial_z\omega\right) = 0$, and for two Kerr black holes $\partial_\rho\omega = -\dfrac{\rho}{f^2}\partial_z\chi$ and $\partial_z\omega = \dfrac{\rho}{f^2}\partial_\rho\chi$, where $\chi$ is the imaginary part of $\mathcal{E}$

Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$ fixed by $f$ and $\omega$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \dfrac{\rho}{4f^2}\left(\left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 - \left(\partial_zf\right)^2\right) - \dfrac{f^2}{4\rho}\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_z\gamma = \dfrac{\rho}{2f^2}\partial_\rho f\,\partial_zf - \dfrac{f^2}{2\rho}\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_z\omega$, and zero on a regular axis; for two Kerr black holes $e^{2\gamma} = \dfrac{\mathrm{Re}\left(D_-D_+^*\right)}{C\,r_1r_2r_3r_4}$, where the star is complex conjugation and the constant $C$ makes $\gamma$ vanish far from the holes; inside an ergoregion, where $f < 0$, $e^{2\gamma}$ is negative with $f$, so $\gamma$ has the imaginary part $\pi/2$ there

coordinates.convention: We use the canonical coordinates of Weyl, Lewis, and Papapetrou, $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ a length fixed by $g_{t\phi}^2 - g_{tt}\,g_{\phi\phi} = \rho^2$, and $z$ a length along the axis. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
